claims.evidence: This is inferred from the context of the cited study (Tovote et al., 2016).

claims.claim: A considerable number of vlPAG single-units (91/245, ~37%) inhibited activity on cue presentation, particularly to danger.
claims.source: Among the vlPAG single-units recorded in our previous study (Wright and McDannald, 2019), a considerable number inhibited activity on cue presentation (91/245,~37% of single-units recorded), particularly to danger.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' prior study.

claims.claim: Rats were trained to nose poke in a central port in order to receive a food pellet from a cup below.
claims.source: Rats were trained to nose poke in a central port in order to receive a food pellet from a cup below.
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral training procedure used in the study.

claims.claim: During fear discrimination, three distinct auditory cues predicted unique foot shock probabilities: danger (p = 1.00), uncertainty (p = 0.375) and safety (p = 0.00).
claims.source: During fear discrimination, three distinct auditory cues predicted unique foot shock probabilities: danger (p = 1.00), uncertainty (p = 0.375) and safety (p = 0.00) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design, shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Fear was measured using a suppression ratio calculated by comparing nose poke rates during baseline and cue periods.
claims.source: Fear was measured using a suppression ratio and was calculated by comparing nose poke rates during baseline and cue periods (Pickens et al., 2009; Berg et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2015; DiLeo et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral measurement method, supported by citations to prior studies using this method.

claims.claim: After eight discrimination sessions, rats were implanted with 16-wire, drivable microelectrode bundles dorsal to the vlPAG.
claims.source: After eight discrimination sessions, rats were implanted with 16-wire, drivable microelectrode bundles dorsal to the vlPAG (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the surgical procedure, with electrode placements shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Following recovery, rats were returned to fear discrimination and activity was recorded.
claims.source: Following recovery, rats were returned to fear discrimination and activity was recorded.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Single-units were isolated and held for the duration of each recording session.
claims.source: Single-units were isolated and held for the duration of each recording session.
claims.evidence: This describes the neural recording methodology.

claims.claim: The electrode bundle was advanced ~40–80 µm between sessions to record from new single-units in subsequent sessions.
claims.source: The electrode bundle was advanced ~40–80 µm between sessions to record from new single-units in subsequent sessions.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for sampling different neurons.

claims.claim: Rats showed excellent discriminative fear: high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and low to safety.
claims.source: Rats showed excellent discriminative fear: high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and low to safety (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study, shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: ANOVA for suppression ratio for the entire 10 s cue using trial-type as a factor revealed a main effect of trial-type (F2,174 = 592.00, p = 2.32×10−78, ηp2 = 0.87, op = 1.00).
claims.source: ANOVA for suppression ratio for the entire 10 s cue using trial-type as a factor (danger, uncertainty and safety) revealed a main effect of trial-type (F2,174 = 592.00, p = 2.32×10−78, ηp2 = 0.87, observed power (op) = 1.00).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: The 95% bootstrap confidence interval did not contain zero for danger vs. uncertainty (Mean = 0.30, 95% CI [0.24, 0.34]) and uncertainty vs. safety (M = 0.50, 95% CI [0.44, 0.56]), indicating full cue discrimination.
claims.source: Indicative of full cue discrimination, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval did not contain zero for danger vs. uncertainty (Mean = 0.30, 95% CI [(lower bound) 0.24, (upper bound) 0.34]) and uncertainty vs. safety (M = 0.50, 95% CI [0.44, 0.56]) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of behavioral data, shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: 245 neurons were recorded in six male Long Evans rats over 88 fear discrimination sessions.
claims.source: We recorded 245 neurons in six male Long Evans rats over 88 fear discrimination sessions.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample size and experimental scope.

claims.claim: 91 neurons (~37% of all neurons recorded) showed significant decreases in firing rate to danger or uncertainty.
claims.source: We identified 91 neurons (~37% of all neurons recorded) showing significant decreases in firing rate to danger or uncertainty.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from neural data analysis.

claims.claim: Visualization of all cue-inhibited neurons revealed heterogeneous inhibition of danger firing during late cue presentation.
claims.source: Visualization of all cue-inhibited neurons revealed heterogeneous inhibition of danger firing during late cue presentation (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of neural data, shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: K-means clustering for all cue-inhibited neurons on early (first 5 s) and late (last 5 s) firing to danger identified two clusters.
claims.source: To determine whether this heterogeneity reflected the activity of two separate populations, we performed k-means clustering for all cue-inhibited neurons on early (first 5 s) and late (last 5 s) firing to danger.
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical method used to identify neuron populations.

claims.claim: The first cluster (n = 45) consisted of neurons that were danger-inhibited early, but danger-excited late, referred to as the Flip population.
claims.source: The first cluster (n = 45) consisted of neurons that were danger-inhibited early, but danger-excited late. These neurons are referred to as the Flip population.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cluster analysis of neural data.

claims.claim: The second cluster (n = 46) consisted of neurons that were danger-inhibited early and late, referred to as the Sustain population.
claims.source: The second cluster (n = 46) consisted of neurons that were danger-inhibited early and late, and are referred to as the Sustain population.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cluster analysis of neural data.

claims.claim: Independent samples t-tests for waveform properties revealed no differences between Flip and Sustain neurons.
claims.source: Independent samples t-tests for waveform properties revealed no differences between Flip and Sustain neurons, indicating these populations could only be distinguished by their function (Figure 1E–G): baseline firing, t89 = 0.95, p = 0.343; half duration, t89 = 0.77, p = 0.444; amplitude ratio t89 = 0.10, p = 0.918.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of neural waveform properties, shown in Figures 1E-G.

claims.claim: Flip and Sustain neuron populations could only be distinguished by their function, not by waveform properties.
claims.source: Independent samples t-tests for waveform properties revealed no differences between Flip and Sustain neurons, indicating these populations could only be distinguished by their function (Figure 1E–G): baseline firing, t89 = 0.95, p = 0.343; half duration, t89 = 0.77, p = 0.444; amplitude ratio t89 = 0.10, p = 0.918.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis showing no waveform differences.

claims.claim: Flip neurons were initially inhibited to uncertainty and danger, but lesser to safety.
claims.source: Flip neurons were initially inhibited to uncertainty and danger, but lesser to safety (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of neural activity patterns, shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: As cue presentation continued, inhibition to uncertainty weakened toward safety and firing to danger switched to excitation in Flip neurons.
claims.source: As cue presentation continued, inhibition to uncertainty weakened toward safety and firing to danger switched to excitation (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of neural activity, shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: ANOVA for normalized firing rate of the 45 Flip neurons revealed main effects of cue (F2,88 = 16.58, p = 7.74×10−7, ηp2 = 0.27, op = 1.00) and bin (F55,2420 = 14.83, p = 1.03×10−114, ηp2 = 0.25, op = 1.00), and a cue x bin interaction (F110,4840 = 7.85, p = 8.89×10−106, ηp2 = 0.15, op = 1.00).
claims.source: ANOVA for normalized firing rate (Z-score) for the 45 Flip neurons [Figure 2A; factors: trial-type (danger, uncertainty and safety) and bin (250 ms bins encompassing: 2 s baseline, 10 s cue, and 2 s delay)] revealed main effects of cue (F2,88 = 16.58, p = 7.74×10−7, ηp2 = 0.27, op = 1.00) and bin (F55,2420 = 14.83, p = 1.03×10−114, ηp2 = 0.25, op = 1.00), but most critically a cue x bin interaction (F110,4840 = 7.85, p = 8.89×10−106, ηp2 = 0.15, op = 1.00).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of neural firing data.

claims.claim: The population pattern of Flip neurons was consistent across individual trials, though late danger excitation was least on the first and last trials.
claims.source: The population pattern was consistent across individual trials, though late danger excitation was least on the first and last trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from trial-by-trial analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claims.claim: Differential firing was not observed to danger vs. uncertainty early (M = 0.04, 95% CI [−0.05, 0.11]) in Flip neurons, but was observed late when danger flipped to excitation (M = 0.35, 95% CI [0.26, 0.42]).
claims.source: Differential firing was not observed to danger vs. uncertainty early (M = 0.04, 95% CI [−0.05, 0.11]), but was observed late when danger flipped to excitation (M = 0.35, 95% CI [0.26, 0.42]) (Figure 2B, plus signs).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from bootstrap confidence interval analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Differential firing was observed to uncertainty vs. safety early (M = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.26,–0.11]) in Flip neurons, but not late (M = −0.05, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.05]).
claims.source: In contrast, differential firing was observed to uncertainty vs. safety early (M = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.26,–0.11]), but not late (M = −0.05, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.05]) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from bootstrap confidence interval analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The 95% bootstrap confidence interval for normalized firing did not contain zero for any cues in either period for Flip neurons, indicating the Flip population was responsive to all cues.
claims.source: Furthermore, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval for normalized firing did not contain zero for any cues in either period (Figure 1B, pound signs), indicating the Flip population was responsive to all cues.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result and interpretation from bootstrap confidence interval analysis.

claims.claim: Sustain neurons showed cue-selective inhibition of firing: danger < uncertainty < safety ≈ 0.
claims.source: Sustain neurons showed cue-selective inhibition of firing: danger < uncertainty < safety ≈ 0.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of neural activity patterns.

claims.claim: The firing pattern of Sustain neurons was observed throughout cue presentation.
claims.source: This firing pattern was observed throughout cue presentation (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of neural activity, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: ANOVA for normalized firing rate of Sustain neurons revealed main effects of cue (F2,86 = 72.25, p = 3.88×10−19, ηp2 = 0.63, op = 1.00) and bin (F55,2365 = 14.91, p = 6.13×10−115, ηp2 = 0.26, op = 1.00), as well as a cue x bin interaction (F110,4730 = 5.24, p = 1.17×10−59, ηp2 = 0.11, op = 1.00).
claims.source: ANOVA for normalized firing rate [Figure 2C; factors maintained from above] revealed main effects of cue (F2,86 = 72.25, p = 3.88×10−19, ηp2 = 0.63, op = 1.00) and bin (F55,2365 = 14.91, p = 6.13×10−115, ηp2 = 0.26, op = 1.00), as well as a cue x bin interaction (F110,4730 = 5.24, p = 1.17×10−59, ηp2 = 0.11, op = 1.00).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of neural firing data.

claims.claim: The population pattern of Sustain neurons was consistent across all trials.
claims.source: The population pattern was consistent across all trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from trial-by-trial analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H.

claims.claim: Selective firing in Sustain neurons was observed early and late in cue presentation.
claims.source: Selective firing was observed early and late in cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of neural activity.

claims.claim: The 95% bootstrap confidence interval for differential firing in Sustain neurons did not contain zero for danger vs. uncertainty (Early: M = −0.24, 95% CI [−0.35,–0.14], Late: M = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.25,–0.11]) and uncertainty vs. safety (Early: M = −0.23, 95% CI [−0.32,–0.15], Late: M = −0.27, 95% CI [−0.35, 0.18]).
claims.source: In support, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval for differential firing did not contain zero for danger vs. uncertainty (Early: M = −0.24, 95% CI [−0.35,–0.14], Late: M = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.25,–0.11]) and uncertainty vs. safety (Early: M = −0.23, 95% CI [−0.32,–0.15], Late: M = −0.27, 95% CI [−0.35, 0.18]) (Figure 2D, plus signs).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from bootstrap confidence interval analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The 95% bootstrap confidence interval for normalized firing in Sustain neurons did not contain zero for danger and uncertainty during both periods, but did contain zero for safety during both periods.
claims.source: Even more, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval for normalized firing did not contain zero for danger and uncertainty during both periods, but did contain zero for safety during both periods (Figure 1D, pound signs).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from bootstrap confidence interval analysis.

claims.claim: Sustain neurons were selectively responsive to danger and uncertainty.
claims.source: Not only was differential firing observed, but Sustain neurons were selectively responsive to danger and uncertainty.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the statistical results showing selective responses.

claims.claim: Flip single-units were biased towards decreased firing to danger during early cue presentation (p(sign) = 9.33×10−9).
claims.source: Flip single-units were biased towards decreased firing to danger [Early: (p(sign) = 9.33×10−9)] and uncertainty [Early: (p(s) = 5.89×10−11)] during early cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis of single-unit data.

claims.claim: Flip single-units were biased towards decreased firing to uncertainty during early cue presentation (p(s) = 5.89×10−11).
claims.source: Flip single-units were biased towards decreased firing to danger [Early: (p(sign) = 9.33×10−9)] and uncertainty [Early: (p(s) = 5.89×10−11)] during early cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis of single-unit data.

claims.claim: Flip neurons were biased towards increased firing to danger during late cue presentation (p(s) = 8.24×10−4).
claims.source: Strikingly, and consistent with the population response, Flip neurons were biased towards increased firing to danger [Late: (p(s) = 8.24×10−4)], but decreased firing to uncertainty [Late: (p(s) = 2.47×10−4)] during late cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis of single-unit data.

claims.claim: Flip neurons were biased towards decreased firing to uncertainty during late cue presentation (p(s) = 2.47×10−4).
claims.source: Strikingly, and consistent with the population response, Flip neurons were biased towards increased firing to danger [Late: (p(s) = 8.24×10−4)], but decreased firing to uncertainty [Late: (p(s) = 2.47×10−4)] during late cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis of single-unit data.

claims.claim: There was no bias away from zero in single-unit Flip neuron firing to safety early or late.
claims.source: Contrary to the population result, there was no bias away from zero in single-unit firing to safety early or late.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis of single-unit data.

claims.claim: Sustain single-units showed no bias in firing to safety in either cue period.
claims.source: Further, Sustain single-units showed no bias in firing to safety in either cue period.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis of single-unit data.

claims.claim: Observing fully differential firing by single-units throughout cue presentation marks Sustain neurons as a candidate for signaling fear output.
claims.source: Observing fully differential firing by single-units throughout cue presentation further marks Sustain neurons as a candidate for signaling fear output.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of neural activity observed.

claims.claim: Linear regression was used to test the degree to which Flip and Sustain neurons signaled fear output and threat probability.
claims.source: We used linear regression for single-unit firing to formally test the degree to which Flip and Sustain neurons signaled fear output and threat probability (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical method used, with results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: For each single-unit, normalized firing rate was calculated for each trial in 1 s bins over the course of cue presentation (14 s total: 2 s pre-cue, 10 s cue, 2 s post-cue).
claims.source: For each single-unit, we calculated the normalized firing rate for each trial (32 total: six danger, six uncertainty shock, 10 uncertainty omission, and 10 safety) in 1 s bins over the course of cue presentation (14 s total: 2 s pre-cue, 10 s cue, 2 s post-cue).
claims.evidence: This describes the data analysis procedure.

claims.claim: Fear output was the suppression ratio on that trial.
claims.source: Fear output was the suppression ratio on that trial.
claims.evidence: This defines the fear output regressor used in the analysis.

claims.claim: Threat probability was the shock probability associated with the cue: danger: 1.00, uncertainty: 0.375 and safety: 0.00.
claims.source: Threat probability was the shock probability associated with the cue: danger: 1.00, uncertainty: 0.375 and safety: 0.00.
claims.evidence: This defines the threat probability regressor used in the analysis.

claims.claim: Single-unit regression revealed an early-to-late switch in threat probability signaling by Flip neurons.
claims.source: Single-unit regression revealed an early-to-late switch in threat probability signaling by Flip neurons (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: ANOVA for beta coefficients during the cue period found a regressor x interval interaction (F9,396 = 3.56, p = 2.85×10−4, ηp2 = 0.075, op = 0.990) for Flip neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, the cue ANOVA found significant main effects, but most critically a regressor x interval interaction (F9,396 = 3.56, p = 2.85×10−4, ηp2 = 0.075, op = 0.990).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA of regression beta coefficients.

claims.claim: The interaction in Flip neurons was driven by negative beta coefficients for fear output and threat probability in two, early cue intervals that gave way to positive beta coefficients specific to threat probability in all late cue intervals.
claims.source: The interaction was driven by negative beta coefficients for fear output and threat probability in two, early cue intervals (95% bootstrap confidence interval did not contain zero, pound signs), that gave way to positive beta coefficients specific to threat probability in all late cue intervals (95% bootstrap confidence interval did not contain zero, pound signs; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical interaction, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Beta coefficients for Flip single-units were not biased away from zero for fear output and threat probability during the first 5 s cue period (Probability Early: p(s) = 0.37, Fear Output Early: p(s) = 0.14).
claims.source: Further supporting the interaction, beta coefficients for Flip single-units were not biased away from zero for fear output and threat probability during the first 5 s cue period [Probability Early: p(s) = 0.37, Fear Output Early: p(s) = 0.14] (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: There was positive bias toward threat probability, but not fear output, during the last 5 s cue period for Flip neurons (Probability Late: p(s) = 2.47×10−4, Fear Output Late: p(s) = 0.77).
claims.source: However, there was positive bias toward threat probability, but not fear output, during the last 5 s cue period [Probability Late: p(s) = 2.47×10−4, Fear Output Late: p(s) = 0.77] (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis, shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Flip neurons do not consistently signal threat probability or fear output in early cue presentation.
claims.source: Fear responses are sustained for the cue duration, yet Flip neurons do not consistently signal threat probability or fear output in early cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the regression analysis results.

claims.claim: The inconsistency in signaling reveals that Flip neurons are not a suitable neural substrate for governing fear output throughout cue presentation.
claims.source: The inconsistency in signaling reveals that Flip neurons are not a suitable neural substrate for governing fear output throughout cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal pattern of neural signaling.

claims.claim: Linear regression revealed consistent signals for fear output and threat probability in Sustain neurons.
claims.source: Linear regression revealed consistent signals for fear output and threat probability in Sustain neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis.

claims.claim: Beta coefficients for Sustain neurons were negative at cue onset for each regressor, and maintained this negativity throughout cue presentation.
claims.source: Beta coefficients were negative at cue onset for each regressor, and maintained this negativity throughout cue presentation (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis, shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: ANOVA for beta coefficients during the cue period found only a main effect of bin (F9,405 = 4.23, p = 2.90×10−5, ηp2 = 0.086, op = 0.997) for Sustain neurons, indicating similar signaling of fear output and threat probability.
claims.source: The cue ANOVA found only a main effect of bin (F9,405 = 4.23, p = 2.90×10−5, ηp2 = 0.086, op = 0.997), indicating similar signaling of fear output and threat probability.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA of regression beta coefficients.

claims.claim: For each regressor over the 10, 1 s cue intervals in Sustain neurons, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval did not contain zero, indicating that fear output and threat probability signaling were observed throughout cue presentation.
claims.source: For each regressor over the 10, 1 s cue intervals, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval did not contain zero, indicating that fear output and threat probability signaling were observed throughout cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from bootstrap confidence interval analysis.

claims.claim: Single-unit beta coefficients for Sustain neurons for each regressor were biased away from zero for fear output and threat probability during early and late cue presentation (Probability Early: p(s) = 1.83×10−6, Late: p(s) = 4.06×10−5; Fear Output Early: p(s) = 0.002, Late: p(s) = 1.56×10−4).
claims.source: Consistent with equivalent signaling of fear output and probability throughout cue presentation, single-unit beta coefficients for each regressor were biased away from zero for fear output and threat probability during early and late cue presentation [Probability (Early: p(s) = 1.83×10−6 and Late: p(s) = 4.06×10−5), Fear Output (Early: p(s) = 0.002 and Late: p(s) = 1.56×10−4)] (Figure 3E & F).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sign test analysis, shown in Figures 3E & F.

claims.claim: Single-unit beta coefficients for threat probability and fear output in Sustain neurons were correlated early and late (Early: R2 = 0.41, p = 2.38×10−6 and Late: R2 = 0.37, p = 9.55×10−6).
claims.source: Further, single-unit beta coefficients for threat probability and fear output were correlated early and late (Early: R2 = 0.41, p = 2.38×10−6 and Late: R2 = 0.37, p = 9.55×10−6).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The majority of Sustain single-units showed negative beta coefficients for both regressors.
claims.source: The majority of Sustain single-units showed negative beta coefficients for both regressors.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the regression analysis results.

claims.claim: Even the extremes of the distribution of Sustain neurons showed signaling for both regressors, albeit in opposing directions.
claims.source: However, even the extremes of the distribution showed signaling for both regressors, albeit in opposing directions.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the regression analysis results.

claims.claim: Sustain neurons signal fear output and threat probability throughout cue presentation.
claims.source: Sustain neurons signal fear output and threat probability throughout cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the regression analysis results.

claims.claim: It is possible that Flip and Sustain single-units are 'tuned' to alternative shock probabilities.
claims.source: Thus, it is possible that Flip and Sustain single-units are 'tuned' to alternative shock probabilities.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of neural tuning.

claims.claim: Single-unit linear regression was performed with the probabilities for danger (1.00) and safety (0.00) maintained, but incrementing the probability assigned to uncertainty from 0 to 1 in 0.125 steps.
claims.source: To test this, we performed single-unit linear regression for normalized firing in each 1 s interval as before, maintaining the probabilities for danger (1.00) and safety (0.00), but incrementing the probability assigned to uncertainty from 0 to 1 in 0.125 steps (0.000, 0.125, 0.250, 0.375, 0.500, 0.625, 0.750, 0.875, and 1.000).
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical method used to test threat tuning.

claims.claim: Flip neurons were tuned to alternative foot shock probabilities and this tuning changed from early to late cue presentation.
claims.source: Flip neurons were tuned to alternative foot shock probabilities and this tuning changed from early to late cue presentation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the threat tuning analysis.

claims.claim: Early threat overestimation (equating uncertainty to danger) gave way to late underestimation (equating uncertainty to safety) in Flip neurons.
claims.source: Early threat overestimation (equating uncertainty to danger) gave way to late underestimation (equating uncertainty to safety).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the threat tuning analysis results.

claims.claim: The tuning curve trough for Flip neurons during early cue presentation occurred at 0.750.
claims.source: The tuning curve trough for early cue presentation occurred at 0.750 (Figure 4A, light pink); overshooting the actual probability of 0.375 (Figure 4A, dashed black line) and exceeding mean fear output (Figure 4A, dashed green line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the threat tuning analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The tuning curve peak for Flip neurons during late cue presentation occurred at 0.250.
claims.source: The tuning curve peak for late cue presentation occurred at 0.250 (Figure 4A, dark pink); undershooting the actual probability (Figure 4A, dashed black line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the threat tuning analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: ANOVA for beta coefficient with factors of time (early vs. late) and uncertainty assignment (9) found both main effects and the interaction to be significant (all F > 13, all p < 0.001) for Flip neurons.
claims.source: ANOVA for beta coefficient with factors of time (early vs. late) and uncertainty assignment (9) found both main effects and the interaction to be significant (all F > 13, all p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA of threat tuning data.

claims.claim: The relative firing patterns of Flip neurons do not approximate the actual probability of foot shock or the pattern of fear output.
claims.source: The relative firing patterns of Flip neurons do not approximate the actual probability of foot shock or the pattern of fear output, and further indicate that these neurons are unlikely to govern fear output.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the threat tuning analysis results.

claims.claim: Flip neurons are unlikely to govern fear output.
claims.source: The relative firing patterns of Flip neurons do not approximate the actual probability of foot shock or the pattern of fear output, and further indicate that these neurons are unlikely to govern fear output.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the threat tuning analysis results.

claims.claim: Sustain neuron tuning consistently fell between the bounds of the actual foot shock probability and the mean fear output, changing only subtly over cue presentation.
claims.source: In contrast, Sustain neuron tuning consistently fell between the bounds of the actual foot shock probability and the mean fear output, changing only subtly over cue presentation (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the threat tuning analysis, shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The trough of the tuning curve for Sustain neurons occurred at an assignment of 0.500 early and at an assignment of 0.625 late.
claims.source: The trough of the tuning curve occurred at an assignment of 0.500 early and at an assignment of 0.625 late.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the threat tuning analysis.

claims.claim: ANOVA for Sustain neurons found a main effect of assignment (F8,360 = 5.66, p = 8.85×10−7, ηp2 = 0.112, op = 1.00) and a time x assignment interaction (F8,360 = 3.25, p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.067, op = 0.971).
claims.source: ANOVA found a main effect of assignment (F8,360 = 5.66, p = 8.85×10−7, ηp2 = 0.112, op = 1.00) and a time x assignment interaction (F8,360 = 3.25, p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.067, op = 0.971).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA of threat tuning data.

claims.claim: The stability of Sustain tuning and the bias toward mean fear output suggests this population as a candidate for fear output.
claims.source: The stability of Sustain tuning and the bias toward mean fear output further suggests this population as a candidate for fear output.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the threat tuning analysis results.

results.result: Rats were trained in a fear discrimination task with three auditory cues predicting different shock probabilities (danger p=1.00, uncertainty p=0.375, safety p=0.00). After training, rats were implanted with microelectrode bundles dorsal to vlPAG and neural activity was recorded during continued discrimination sessions. Rats showed excellent discriminative fear behavior with suppression ratios graded by threat level.
results.evaluation: The experimental design and behavioral results are well-documented with appropriate statistical support (C28, C29). The methods are clearly described including subject details (C125-C132), behavioral training (C20-C22), surgical procedures (C23, C127-C128), and recording methodology (C24-C26). The behavioral discrimination was statistically significant with proper effect sizes and confidence intervals reported.

results.result: K-means clustering of 91 cue-inhibited vlPAG neurons based on early and late danger responses identified two distinct functional populations: Flip neurons (n=45) that switched from early inhibition to late excitation, and Sustain neurons (n=46) that maintained inhibition throughout. These populations could only be distinguished by their functional responses, not by waveform properties.
results.evaluation: The clustering analysis is appropriately applied and yields two clear populations (C33-C35). Statistical tests confirm no differences in waveform properties between populations (C36), supporting the conclusion that they are functionally distinct (C37). The methodology for identifying cue-inhibited neurons and clustering approach is clearly described.

results.result: Flip neurons showed initial inhibition to danger and uncertainty cues that transitioned to excitation for danger during late cue presentation. Early in the cue, differential firing distinguished uncertainty from safety but not danger from uncertainty. Late in the cue, danger flipped to excitation and became differentiated from uncertainty. Single-unit analyses confirmed these population-level patterns.
results.evaluation: The temporal dynamics of Flip neurons are well-characterized with strong statistical support including significant cue × bin interactions (C40), bootstrap confidence intervals (C42-C44), and sign tests at the single-unit level (C53-C57). The pattern is consistent across trials (C41) and supported by multiple analytical approaches.

results.result: Sustain neurons showed graded, cue-selective inhibition (danger < uncertainty < safety ≈ 0) that was maintained throughout cue presentation. This differential firing pattern was observed both early and late in the cue period, with neurons selectively responsive to danger and uncertainty but not safety. Single-unit analyses confirmed population-level patterns.
results.evaluation: The characterization of Sustain neurons is robust with strong statistical support including significant main effects and interactions (C47), bootstrap confidence intervals showing differential firing throughout cue presentation (C50-C51), and consistent patterns across trials (C48). Single-unit sign tests confirm selective responsiveness (C60).

results.result: Linear regression analysis revealed that Flip neurons showed an early-to-late switch in threat probability signaling. Early in cue presentation, Flip neurons did not consistently signal threat probability or fear output. Late in cue presentation, they showed positive bias toward threat probability but not fear output. This temporal inconsistency indicates Flip neurons are not suitable substrates for governing fear output throughout cue presentation.
results.evaluation: The regression analysis is appropriately conducted with clear definition of regressors (C64-C65). Statistical results show significant regressor × interval interaction (C67) and the interpretation is supported by bootstrap confidence intervals (C68) and sign tests (C69-C70). The conclusion that Flip neurons are unsuitable for fear output is logically derived from the temporal inconsistency in signaling (C71-C72).

results.result: Linear regression revealed that Sustain neurons consistently signaled both fear output and threat probability throughout cue presentation. Beta coefficients were negative for both regressors and maintained throughout the cue period. Single-unit analyses showed biases away from zero for both regressors during early and late periods, with significant correlations between threat probability and fear output coefficients.
results.evaluation: The regression analysis demonstrates consistent signaling with appropriate statistics including ANOVA showing only main effect of bin (C75), bootstrap confidence intervals throughout cue presentation (C76), sign tests showing biases in both periods (C77), and significant correlations between regressors (C78). The conclusion that Sustain neurons signal both fear output and threat probability is well-supported.

results.result: Threat tuning analysis revealed that Flip neurons were tuned to alternative shock probabilities that changed from early to late cue presentation. Early tuning showed threat overestimation (trough at 0.750), while late tuning showed underestimation (peak at 0.250). This pattern does not approximate actual shock probability or fear output, further indicating Flip neurons are unlikely to govern fear output.
results.evaluation: The threat tuning analysis is methodologically sound (C83) with clear results showing temporal changes in tuning (C84-C87). Statistical support includes significant main effects and interactions (C88). The interpretation that Flip neurons do not approximate actual probability or fear output is justified by the tuning curve positions relative to actual probability and behavioral output (C89-C90).

results.result: Threat tuning analysis of Sustain neurons showed stable tuning that consistently fell between actual shock probability and mean fear output, changing only subtly over cue presentation. The tuning trough occurred at 0.500 early and 0.625 late, exceeding the actual probability of 0.375 and better approximating fear output. This stability suggests Sustain neurons as candidates for fear output.
results.evaluation: The threat tuning analysis for Sustain neurons shows appropriate statistical support (C93) and the tuning positions are clearly documented (C92). The interpretation that stable tuning biased toward fear output suggests these neurons as candidates for fear output is reasonable (C94, C105), though the authors appropriately note this is correlational evidence.

results.result: Flip neurons may provide information about anticipated timing of foot shock rather than fear output. Peak activity occurred just prior to shock presentation and declined shortly after. This pattern resembles previously reported 'Ramping' neurons and is consistent with studies showing shifts from prefrontal to periaqueductal activity as threats become more proximate, suggesting a role for vlPAG in threat timing.
results.evaluation: While the temporal pattern of Flip neuron activity is well-documented (C96) and the comparison to prior work is appropriate (C97-C98), the interpretation regarding threat timing is largely speculative (C95, C99, C100). The claim that Flip neurons signal threat timing lacks direct experimental evidence and is inferred from temporal patterns. This represents a reasonable hypothesis but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Sustain neurons represent a complete neural correlate for fear output in vlPAG. Their activity pattern complies with basic assumptions: they decreased firing to threat-related cues but not safety, fully discriminated between all cue types throughout presentation, and the differential firing pattern reflected fear output. However, causal evidence that these neurons drive fear responses is lacking.
results.evaluation: The characterization of Sustain neurons as a neural correlate for fear output is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including temporal dynamics (C102-C103), differential firing patterns (C5-C7), and consistency between population and single-unit levels (C104). The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation that this is correlational evidence without causal manipulation (C106). The conclusion is justified given the data but correctly qualified.

results.result: The results are partially consistent with the disinhibition mechanism theory of vlPAG function. While some Sustain neurons had high baseline firing rates consistent with GABAergic interneurons, many had low baseline rates. This heterogeneity suggests cue-inhibited neurons are not uniformly GABAergic interneurons and that vlPAG likely utilizes both disinhibition and independent signaling via cue-excited and cue-inhibited projection populations.
results.evaluation: The observations regarding baseline firing rate heterogeneity are clearly documented (C111-C112) and the inference that neurons are not uniformly GABAergic is reasonable given this evidence (C113). The interpretation that results are consistent with an alternative model incorporating both mechanisms is appropriately qualified as speculative (C114-C115) while being grounded in the observed data. The discussion appropriately contextualizes findings within existing theoretical frameworks.

results.result: Prior work established that vlPAG mediates fear responses and that cue-excited neurons signal threat probability rather than fear output. Cue-inhibited neurons have been observed previously, with optogenetic inhibition promoting freezing. The authors' prior study found ~37% of vlPAG neurons were cue-inhibited, motivating the current investigation.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize established knowledge and prior findings with appropriate citations (C1, C9-C12, C17-C18). The authors' prior work is correctly referenced (C2, C13-C16, C19) and provides appropriate context for the current study. This background establishes the rationale for investigating cue-inhibited neurons.

results.result: The findings expand understanding of vlPAG functional diversity beyond previously identified cue-excited populations. The diversity of information signals in vlPAG is surprising given expectations, and understanding factors determining vlPAG neuron function will be essential for understanding neural mechanisms of adaptive and maladaptive threat behavior, particularly given emerging evidence of vlPAG involvement in psychiatric disorders.
results.evaluation: The summary of prior findings is accurate (C116-C117) and the claim that current findings expand functional diversity is justified (C118, C120). The interpretation regarding surprising diversity (C122) and future directions (C124) are reasonable given the data. The connection to psychiatric disorders is appropriately supported by citation (C123). These represent appropriate contextualization and interpretation of the findings.
